readings.title: A cycle route meets a school gate
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A council planned a cycle route along a road used by families each morning. A drawing showed enough space, but people worried about the school entrance. The central difficulty was crowding at the school gate. Parents stopped briefly near the gate while children crossed the pavement, creating a conflict that a standard road map did not show. The organizers knew that a tidy plan in an office might not match what happened in an ordinary week.

The group first tried morning observations of the entrance. Planners watched arrivals with school staff and cyclists, recording where people waited and when the busiest minutes occurred. They therefore listened to people who used the place at different times, including those who seldom attended formal meetings.

The trial showed a short section needed a different layout. Most of the route could follow the original plan, but the area beside the gate required a clearer crossing and slower movement. In response, the group adopted a separated approach and marked crossing. The council changed that section, then asked families to describe any new difficulty during the first term. The notes did not remove every disagreement, but they made the reasons for the next decision easier to explain.

The broader lesson was clear: safe routes depend on the busiest moments. A route that works at noon may fail during a brief school arrival period, so time matters as much as space. Keeping a record of small changes also helped the team distinguish a temporary setback from a lasting problem. For the people involved in a cycle route meets a school gate, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: A ferry timetable for two kinds of passenger
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A river ferry served commuters and weekend visitors. Its printed schedule listed departures, yet people often asked when the last boat would leave. The central difficulty was weekday and weekend times looked too similar. The columns were close together and the final crossing had a different time on public holidays. A first impression was not enough to tell the whole story, because different people approached the service in different ways.

The group first tried a timetable trial with clearer headings. Staff printed separate panels for weekdays and weekends and asked new passengers to find a final return crossing. The team compared comments with direct observations rather than assuming that the loudest opinion represented everyone.

The trial showed clear headings reduced missed departures. Passengers located the right column faster, although a few still overlooked the public holiday note. In response, the group adopted a prominent holiday warning and web update. The ferry office placed the exception beside the last departure and kept a dated online version for unexpected changes. Some suggestions were inexpensive, while others would have required a change to staffing or equipment.

The broader lesson was clear: timetables should answer a real journey question. Staff judged the design by whether travellers could plan a return, not merely by whether every time was printed. The final proposal remained open to revision when new information became available. For the people involved in a ferry timetable for two kinds of passenger, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: Finding a safer crossing
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents asked for a new crossing near a health centre. The nearest marked crossing was legal but required a long detour. The central difficulty was pedestrians crossing at an unmarked bend. Many people chose the direct route, including visitors with walking aids, because the alternative added several minutes. Several participants valued the original aim even though they questioned the first method chosen to reach it.

The group first tried a count of routes at different hours. Engineers recorded where people actually crossed and how traffic speed changed during clinic opening times. Short conversations after the activity revealed details that a written form had failed to capture.

The trial showed demand followed the clinic schedule. The busiest crossing period was not the general rush hour but the short interval before appointments began. In response, the group adopted a crossing closer to the entrance. The council adjusted the location and added clear signs, then planned another count after the new arrangement opened. The people responsible made their limits clear and invited others to describe any unintended effects.

The broader lesson was clear: pedestrian design should reflect actual routes. Telling people to take a long detour was less effective than understanding why they preferred the shorter path. This approach gave the group a practical basis for its next round of work. For the people involved in finding a safer crossing, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: Parcel deliveries on a narrow street
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Shops on a narrow street needed frequent deliveries. Drivers often stopped where pedestrians had to step into the road. The central difficulty was unplanned delivery stops blocking the footway. The street had no agreed unloading window, so vans arrived at the same time as shoppers and schoolchildren. The project began on a small scale so that its organizers could learn before making a permanent commitment.

The group first tried a shared morning delivery period. Shop owners and drivers tried a short time slot before the busiest pedestrian hours and recorded delays. They noted both benefits and costs, including the time that volunteers or staff needed to give.

The trial showed some deliveries could move without harming trade. Several shops adapted easily, while one bakery needed a separate early delivery to keep food fresh. In response, the group adopted a marked loading point with one exception. The council reserved space near the shops and allowed the bakery an earlier slot after discussing its specific need. The public summary described what had changed and what questions had not yet been answered.

The broader lesson was clear: street rules work best with practical exceptions. A simple schedule reduced conflicts, but listening to different businesses prevented the rule from creating a new problem. Readers could therefore judge the decision by its evidence rather than by a promise of perfect results. For the people involved in parcel deliveries on a narrow street, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A road design may seem safe when it is examined on a quiet afternoon. Conditions can be very different outside a school at the start of the day. Parents stop briefly, children cross the pavement and cyclists approach the entrance at the same time. Before marking a new cycle route, planners watched these movements during the busiest minutes. They found that only a short section needed a different arrangement. A clearer crossing and a slower approach could reduce conflict without changing the whole route. The council then asked families to report new difficulties after the work was completed. Good transport planning considers when people travel as well as where they travel.
translation.explanation: 注意when与where的并列对照及without doing结构。
translation.referenceAnswer: 在安静的下午观察时，一项道路设计可能显得安全。但每天开始时，学校门口的情况会很不一样：家长短暂停车，孩子穿过人行道，骑车人同时接近校门。规划人员在标出新自行车路线前，观察了最繁忙几分钟的行动。他们发现只有一小段需要采用不同安排。更清晰的过街处和放慢速度的入口可以减少冲突，而不必改变整条路线。施工完成后，市政部门请家长报告新的困难。好的交通规划既考虑人们何时出行，也考虑他们走向哪里。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to a town transport office about a proposed cycle route near a school. Explain when observations should be made, what should be recorded, and how families could comment after opening.
writing.explanation: 范文覆盖高峰时段观察、记录内容和开放后反馈。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Transport Officer,
I support a safer cycle route, but the section near the school gate needs special attention. Please observe it during the fifteen minutes before classes begin and again when children leave. A drawing made in a quiet afternoon may miss the busiest movements. Observers could record where parents stop, where children cross and how cyclists approach the entrance.
The office could then mark a clear crossing and consider a slower approach for this short section. Families and cyclists should be shown the proposed layout before construction. After the route opens, a simple online form and a notice at the school could invite comments about any new difficulty. Reviewing those reports after one term would help the town decide whether a further adjustment is needed.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
